Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon clearly, if at all.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can probably relax:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
The most significant factor is the Sun's position. With the Sun at an altitude of **43.368 degrees**, it is high in the sky. At this angle, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight (Rayleigh scattering), creating a very bright blue sky. 

Even though the Moon is technically "above the horizon" at 30 degrees, the sheer intensity of the daylight will wash out the Moon's surface details. To the naked eye, the Moon would appear as a very faint, ghostly white smudge—or it would be completely invisible against the glare of the bright sky.

### 2. The Moon's Phase and Position
The Moon is **58.18% illuminated** (a Waxing Gibbous). While a gibbous moon is usually quite bright, its position at an azimuth of **232.237 degrees** means it is in the **Southwest** part of the sky. 

Since the Sun is at an azimuth of **85.647 degrees** (East/Southeast), the Moon is currently "behind" you or to your side relative to the Sun's position. While it isn't directly in front of the Sun (which would make it harder to see), the general brightness of the morning sky in Lagos at that time of day is usually enough to mask a moon that isn't at full illumination.

### 3. Atmospheric Conditions
You mentioned the sky is clear. While a clear sky helps visibility, it also means there are no clouds to "block" the Moon, but it also means there is nothing to dim the Sun's glare. In bright daylight, a clear sky actually makes it *harder* to see faint objects because there is no haze to soften the contrast.

### The Verdict
Because the Sun is so high (over 40 degrees), the "sky brightness" is at its peak. Unless you have extremely high-contrast vision or the Moon happens to be exceptionally bright that specific day, **it will likely be invisible to your unaided eyes.**

You can breathe a sigh of relief—the Sun is doing most of the work for you!
